Summary:
In 374, courts, towns and local coalitions around the Mediterranean, Black Sea, Caspian and North Sea affect one another. Roman roads and grain ships connect distant fields to military camps, while passes and crossings link imperial provinces with steppe, forest and desert. Merchants, envoys, soldiers and displaced households carry reports, but news is incomplete and not always reliable. Leaders must choose within the food, horses, manpower and credit they can actually command.

The Roman courts share imperial legitimacy while facing different pressures. Valentinian relies on networks across Italy, Gaul, Britain and North Africa; Valens draws on the Balkans, Asia Minor, Syria and Egypt. Italy and Constantinople both need reliable grain. Garrison and field forces need pay, animals and transport, and officials must deliver collections to camps. Moving a mobile army leaves another frontier exposed. Orders travel through roads, ports, documents and local elites. Harsh discipline can restore service, but can also encourage officials to conceal shortages.

Rhine and Danube problems differ. Franks and Alamanni compete, while Burgundians and Lombards have their own enemies. One joint operation does not represent permanent agreement by every chief. Roman markets, offices, gifts and settlement terms make the frontier a place of cooperation as well as violence. North of the Danube, anger over Roman fort building and distrust of commanders intensify Quadian and Jazygian tensions. Chiefs demand guarantees and Roman guards fear retaliation. Meeting security, captives and reopened markets all belong in negotiation. A spoken promise over a banquet cannot by itself end distrust; each leader needs conditions followers will accept.

The eastern court must preserve Danube guards while attending to Antioch, Armenia and Persia. Churchmen, officers and provincial elites do not always share an interest. Doctrine can affect appointments and allegiance, while disputes about grain may take religious form. Valens cannot afford discipline that removes both local supply and usable troops. Shapur II relies on Ctesiphon, Mesopotamian irrigation and the Iranian plateau. Noble cavalry, priests and regional rulers expect protection and returns. Nisibis and western agreements offer diplomatic leverage, while fighting Kushans and Kidara limits the resources available for western concentration.

On the northern Black Sea and steppe, horses, grain and safe camps matter more immediately than sweeping border claims. Beler coordinates Alan chiefs around Uspe while facing Huns and Bosporans. Balamber's riders can gather and move quickly but still need water, pasture, remounts and food. New partners require credible rewards rather than intimidation alone. Ermanaric connects Serimum, crossings, farmland and subordinate leaders under pressure from both east and Black Sea approaches. All can fight, ally or seek bounded truces, but dependants and grain carts move slower than a vanguard. Destroying too many settlements removes the victor's own supplies.

Athanaric and Fritigern hold separate hostile positions. Apulum's fields, woods and Danube routes support Athanaric; boats, markets and camps around Troesmis sustain Fritigern. Leaders answer to religion, honor and food needs together. Rome remains a negotiating partner and Gothic contacts can provide intelligence. Rivers are obstacles as well as routes of exchange and movement. Boats, stores and envoys preserve options that a single battlefield success cannot guarantee.

Panticapaeum and the Bosporan ports need both shipping and inland grain. Alan and Greuthungian wars threaten the hinterland while eastern Roman friendship keeps maritime contact possible. Merchants seek predictable cargo movement, garrisons need stores and farmers fear excessive collection. A royal order cannot erase those different interests. Restoring a route or returning captives may help the town more than pursuit of a distant opponent.

North Sea and Scandinavian sailing has equally concrete limits. Angles, Saxons, Danes and Geats have different landing places, fields and kin partners. Vessels carry traders, fishers and armed parties. Taking crews removes farm labor, and delayed return harms stores. Wind, tide, repairs and drinking water can change plans. Chiefs need agreed voyage length, distributions and aid before a joint expedition turns into a lasting feud.

Britain and the Irish Sea do not form one united front. Pictish and Hibernian leaders face Rome, while Votadini are friendly to Rome and at war with Hibernians. Households around Alata, Eblana and Corda have distinct farming, pastoral and coastal interests. Niall and Gartnait require support from local chiefs; Padern balances external assistance with local jurisdiction. Raids can bring wealth but also lose crews and invite retaliation. Ransom, suspended attacks, repairs and markets are practical political tools alongside fighting.

The Caucasus links steppe riders, valley courts and ports. Duin, Mtskheta, Gabala and Archaeopolis rely on different roads and local elites. Darial routes and coastal Caspian passages have different controllers; one vague alliance cannot settle every right of passage. Armenia maintains contacts with both empires, Kartli fights Lazica and Arran fights Maskut. Courts need pass warnings without stopping valley harvests. Outside garrisons may protect but also demand transport and food. Local leaders therefore want guarantees about numbers, duration and provisions.

Around Syria and Mesopotamia, Mavia's kin, Hira's court and the coalition at Dumatha each negotiate war and protection. Palmyra, Hira and oasis wells link herds, farms and caravans. A blocked well can stop an army. Service, rewards, captives and religious concerns can be negotiated together, but promises require kin willing to implement them. Merchants seek reopened roads, followers seek prizes and courts need both standing and supply.

Bukhara and Karnasa likewise depend on valleys, oases, passes and coin credit. Kipunada and Kidara both need local elite cooperation, while Persian pressure makes eastern wars hard to separate. Riders can threaten routes, but merchants and landholders compare the protection each ruler offers. Collection that ruins irrigation, religious property or trading credit can leave the next campaign without food.

Smaller forest, river and steppe polities need room to choose. Bozh, Perbund, Lekh and Roderic cannot let one neighboring dispute consume every household. Kasagos, Kutilzis and Vannius must balance water, grazing, cultivation and powerful neighbors. Shared language or kin does not guarantee shared interests, and friendship does not remove supply obligations. Protection, credible agreements and local support shape long-term choices. Preserving people, food, routes and credit leaves room for further negotiation and action.

[Cities, status and judgment] In the Roman provinces, inhabitants encounter governors, local officials and influential patrons. A complaint can have different consequences according to status, connections and jurisdiction. A gap may open between a procedure described by law and the coercion used by an official; reports of investigations in Rome and other cities can therefore cause fear. An elite household worries that an accusation will destroy its standing, while a person with fewer resources first asks whether witnesses, a guarantor or an intermediary can be found. Frontier chiefs and royal courts also handle injuries, property and captives, often relying on kin and compensation that can actually be delivered. Imperial courts, ecclesiastical mediation and local custom do not provide one identical experience of justice for everyone.

[Households, food and care] Grain, animals and transport labour taken for an army are also resources needed for winter, sowing and tending the sick. Fields, herds, fisheries and markets contribute differently in each region; salt, fuel and vessels for preserving food are not equally available. Siege or a closed route can combine scarcity with dirty water, crowding and disease. An injured person needs care without any guarantee that a trained practitioner or sufficient remedies are nearby. Relatives, neighbours, churches and wealthy households may help, but war can exhaust their means as well. What remains after a delivery of grain, and how people will live until harvest, can determine whether inhabitants stay more decisively than an entry recording that collection was completed.

[Marriage, kinship and dependence] Marriage may connect courts and chiefs, yet involves property, the standing of spouses, children's inheritance and support after widowhood. Roman law, ecclesiastical counsel and different family customs need not answer every question alike. A parent's undertaking does not mean every relative accepts the same sacrifice; dependants compare who can actually protect them. Landholders, cultivators, wage workers, slaves and captives have different rights, and leaving land or a master entails unequal risks. When an army changes control, inhabitants need to know who recognizes their property, obligations and family relationships. A ruler who overlooks those questions may gain a district on a map while losing the cooperation required to feed and govern it.

[Exchange, letters and rumours] Roman gold, other coins and local exchange connect markets, while distant traders also depend on agents, credit and people carrying documents. A stated sum still requires weighing, delivery and acknowledgment; arrival of goods does not settle every partner's share. Sogdian commercial letters from the east combine news of disorder, delayed caravans and instructions about funds at home, allowing distant events to alter immediate lending and travel. Official couriers, arrivals at a port and displaced people each know different fragments. Documents may establish the identity behind an order, but a private report still requires comparison with other sources. Who guarantees the account, and who benefits from alarm, help determine whether it can support a consequential decision.

[Equipment and labour] Armourers, boatbuilders and carriers need materials, payment and time. Taking a skilled worker for military service can also delay farm tools, wagons and repairs to walls. Supply depends on these connected tasks, as well as on precious metal held in a treasury.
